A Message-Passing Receiver for BICM-OFDM over Unknown Clustered-Sparse Channels

Philip Schniter* ††thanks: Please direct all correspondence to Prof. Philip Schniter, Dept. ECE, The Ohio State University, 2015 Neil Ave., Columbus OH 43210, e-mail: schniter@ece.osu.edu, phone 614.247.6488, fax 614.292.7596.††thanks: This work has been supported in part by NSF grant CCF-1018368 and DARPA/ONR grant N66001-10-1-4090, and an allocation of computing time from the Ohio Supercomputer Center.
August 24, 2026
Abstract

We propose a factor-graph-based approach to joint channel-estimation-and-decoding (JCED) of bit-interleaved coded orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (BICM-OFDM). In contrast to existing designs, ours is capable of exploiting not only sparsity in sampled channel taps but also clustering among the large taps, behaviors which are known to manifest at larger communication bandwidths. In order to exploit these channel-tap structures, we adopt a two-state Gaussian mixture prior in conjunction with a Markov model on the hidden state. For loopy belief propagation, we exploit a “generalized approximate message passing” (GAMP) algorithm recently developed in the context of compressed sensing, and show that it can be successfully coupled with soft-input soft-output decoding, as well as hidden Markov inference, through the standard sum-product framework. For NN subcarriers and any channel length L<NL<N, the resulting JCED-GAMP scheme has a computational complexity of only 𝒪⁡(N​log2​N+N​|𝕊|)\mathcal{O}(N\log_{2}N+N|\mathbb{S}|), where |𝕊||\mathbb{S}| is the constellation size. Numerical experiments using IEEE 802.15.4a channels show that our scheme yields BER performance within 1 dB of the known-channel bound and 3-4 dB better than soft equalization based on LMMSE and LASSO.

I Introduction

When designing a digital communications receiver, it is common to model the effects of multipath propagation in discrete time using a convolutive linear channel that, in the slow-fading scenario, can be characterized by a fixed impulse response {xj}j=0L−1\{x_{j}\}_{j=0}^{L-1} over the duration of one codeword. When the communication bandwidth is sufficiently low, the “taps” {xj}j=0L−1\{x_{j}\}_{j=0}^{L-1} are well modeled as independent complex Gaussian random variables, resulting in the “uncorrelated Rayleigh-fading” and “uncorrelated Rician-fading” models that have dominated the wireless communications literature for many decades [1]. For receiver design, the Gaussian tap assumption is very convenient because the optimal estimation scheme is well known to be linear [2]. As the communication bandwidth increases, however, the channel taps are no longer well-modeled as Gaussian nor independent. Rather, they tend to be heavy-tailed or “sparse” in that only a few values in {xj}j=0L−1\{x_{j}\}_{j=0}^{L-1} have significant amplitude [3, 4, 5, 6]. Moreover, groups of large taps are often clustered together in lag jj. These behaviors are both a blessing and a curse: a blessing because, of all tap distributions, the independent Gaussian one is most detrimental to capacity [7], but a curse because optimal channel estimation becomes non-linear and thus receiver design becomes more complicated.

Recently, there have been many attempts to apply breakthrough non-linear estimation techniques from the field of “compressive sensing” [8] (e.g., LASSO [9, 10]) to the wireless channel estimation problem. We refer to this approach as “compressed channel sensing” (CCS), after the recent comprehensive overview [11]. The CCS literature generally takes a decoupled approach to the problem of channel estimation and data decoding, in that pilot-symbol knowledge is first exploited for sparse-channel estimation, after which the channel estimate is used for data decoding. However, this decoupled approach is known to be suboptimal [12].

The considerations above motivate a joint approach to structured-sparse-channel-estimation and decoding that offers both near-optimal decoding performance and low implementation complexity. In this paper, we propose exactly such a scheme. In particular, we focus on orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) with bit-interleaved coded modulation (BICM), and propose a novel factor-graph-based receiver that leverages recent results in “generalized approximate message passing” (GAMP) [13], soft-input/soft-output (SISO) decoding [14], and structured-sparse estimation [15]. Our receiver assumes a clustered-sparse channel-tap prior constructed using a two-state Gaussian mixture with a Markov model on the hidden tap state. The scheme that we propose has only 𝒪⁡(N​log2​N+N​|𝕊|)\mathcal{O}(N\log_{2}N\!+\!N|\mathbb{S}|) complexity, where NN denotes the number of subcarriers and |𝕊||\mathbb{S}| denotes the constellation size, facilitating large values of NN and channel length L<NL\!<\!N (e.g., we use N=1024N\!=\!1024 and L=256L\!=\!256 for our numerical results). For rich non-line-of-sight (NLOS) channels generated according to the IEEE 802.15.4a standard [16], our numerical experiments show bit error rate (BER) performance within 11 dB of the known-channel bound and 33–44 dB better than soft equalization based on LMMSE and LASSO.

We now place our work in the context of existing factor-graph designs. Factor-graph based joint channel-estimation and decoding (JCED) was proposed more than a decade ago (see, e.g., the early overview [17]). To calculate the messages passed among the nodes of the factor graph, first instincts suggest to apply the standard “sum-product algorithm” (SPA) [18, 19, 20]. Exact SPA on the JCED factor graph is computationally infeasible, however, and so it must be approximated. For this, there are many options, since many well-known iterative inference algorithms can themselves be recognized as SPA approximations, e.g., the expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm [21], particle filtering [22], variational (or “mean-field”) techniques [23], and even steepest descent [24]. Moreover, because the JCED factor graph is loopy, even non-approximate SPA is not guaranteed to yield the correct output distributions, because exact inference is NP hard [25]. It is perhaps not surprising that, amidst this uncertainty about exact SPA and its “best” approximation, a number of different factor-graph approaches to JCED over frequency-selective channels have been proposed (e.g., [26, 27, 28, 29]).

Our approach differs from existing factor-graph JCED designs in that it uses 1) a sparse (i.e., non-Gaussian) channel-tap prior, 2) a clustered (i.e., non-independent) channel-tap prior, and 3) a state-of-the-art SPA approximation known as “generalized approximate message passing” (GAMP), which has been shown to admit rigorous analysis as N,L→∞N,L\!\rightarrow\!\infty [13]. In fact, we conjecture that the success of our method is due in large part to the principled approximations used within GAMP. We also note that, although we focus on the case of clustered-sparse channels, our approach could be applied to non-sparse (i.e., Gaussian) or non-clustered (i.e., independent) channel-taps or, e.g., non-sparse channels with unknown length LL [26], with minor modifications of our assumed channel prior.

Finally, we mention that this work is an evolution of our earlier work [30, 31] that was limited to an exactly sparse channel, that did not exploit clustering, and that was based on the “relaxed belief propagation” (RBP) algorithm [32], which has higher implementation complexity than GAMP. For example, the JCED scheme from [30, 31] has complexity 𝒪⁡(N​L+N​|𝕊|)\mathcal{O}(NL\!+\!N|\mathbb{S}|), which grows with the channel length LL.

Our paper is organized as follows. In Section II we detail our assumptions on the OFDM system and the channel prior, and provide an illustrative example of clustered-sparse behavior with the IEEE 802.15.4a channel model. In Section III we detail our GAMP-based JCED approach, in Section IV we report the results of our simulation study, and in Section V we conclude.

II System Model

II-A The BICM-OFDM model

We consider an OFDM system with NN subcarriers, each modulated by a QAM symbol from a 2M2^{M}-ary unit-energy constellation 𝕊\mathbb{S}. Of the NN subcarriers, NpN_{\textsf{p}} are dedicated as pilots,11 1 For our GAMP decoder, we recommend Np=0N_{\textsf{p}}\!=\!0; see Section IV. and the remaining Nd≜N−NpN_{\textsf{d}}\!\triangleq\!N\!-\!N_{\textsf{p}} are used to transmit a total of MtM_{\textsf{t}} training bits and Md≜Nd​M−MtM_{\textsf{d}}\!\triangleq\!N_{\textsf{d}}M\!-\!M_{\textsf{t}} coded/interleaved data bits. The data bits are generated by encoding MiM_{\textsf{i}} information bits using a rate-RR coder, interleaving them, and partitioning the resulting Mc≜Mi/RM_{\textsf{c}}\!\triangleq\!M_{\textsf{i}}/R bits among an integer number Q≜Mc/MdQ\!\triangleq\!M_{\textsf{c}}/M_{\textsf{d}} of OFDM symbols. We note that the resulting scheme has a spectral efficiency of η≜Md​R/N\eta\!\triangleq\!M_{\textsf{d}}R/N information bits per channel use (bpcu).

To simplify the development, we assume that Q=1Q=1 in the sequel (but not in the simulations), and drop the index [q][q] for brevity.

II-B A clustered-sparse tap prior

Empirical studies [3, 4, 5, 6] have suggested that, when the baud rate T−1T^{-1} is sufficiently large, the channel taps {xj}\{x_{j}\} are “sparse” in that the tap distributions tend to be heavy tailed. The same empirical studies suggest that large taps tend to be clustered in the lag domain. Furthermore, both the sparsity and clustering behaviors can be lag-dependent, such as when the receiver’s timing-synchronization mechanism aligns the first strong multipath arrivals with a particular reference lag jj. A concrete example of these behaviors will be given in Section II-C.

Since our message-passing-based receiver design is inherently Bayesian, we seek a prior on the taps {xj}\{x_{j}\} that is capable of representing this lag-dependent clustered sparsity. For this purpose, we assume a two-state Gaussian mixture (GM2) prior,22 2 The message passing algorithm described in Section III-B can also handle non-Gaussian mixtures and/or mixtures with more than two terms.

p⁡(xj)\displaystyle p(x_{j}) =\displaystyle= (1−λj)​𝒞​𝒩​(xj,0,νj0)+λj​𝒞​𝒩​(xj,0,νj1),\displaystyle(1-\lambda_{j})\mathcal{CN}(x_{j};0,\nu^{0}_{j})+\lambda_{j}\mathcal{CN}(x_{j};0,\nu^{1}_{j}), (6)

where νj0≥0\nu_{j}^{0}\!\geq\!0 denotes the variance while in the “small” state, νj1>νj0\nu_{j}^{1}\!>\!\nu_{j}^{0} denotes the variance while in the “big” state, and λj≜Pr{dj=1}\lambda_{j}\!\triangleq\!\Pr\{d_{j}\!=\!1\} denotes the prior probability of xjx_{j} being in the “big” state. Here, we use dj∈{0,1}d_{j}\!\in\!\{0,1\} to denote the hidden state, implying the state-conditional pdf p⁡(xj|dj)=𝒞​𝒩​(xj,0,νjdj).p(x_{j}\,|\,d_{j})=\mathcal{CN}(x_{j};0,\nu^{d_{j}}_{j}).

For example, if xjx_{j} was presumed to be a “sparse” tap, then we would choose λj≪1\lambda_{j}\!\ll\!1 and νj1≫νj0\nu_{j}^{1}\!\gg\!\nu_{j}^{0} in (6). If, on the other hand, xjx_{j} is presumed to be (non-sparse) Rayleigh-fading, we would choose λj=1\lambda_{j}\!=\!1 and set νj1\nu_{j}^{1} equal to the tap variance, noting that νj0\nu_{j}^{0} becomes inconsequential. If xjx_{j} is presumed to be Nakagami-fading or similar, we could fit the GM2 parameters [λj,νj0,νj1][\lambda_{j},\nu_{j}^{0},\nu_{j}^{1}] appropriately using the EM algorithm, as described in [34, p. 435]. The GM2 prior has been used successfully in many other non-Gaussian inference problems (see, e.g., [35]), and our premise here is that the GM2 model achieves a good balance between fidelity and tractability when modeling channel taps as well.

To capture the big-tap clustering behavior, we employ a hidden Markov model (HMM). For this, we model the tap states {dj}j=0L−1\{d_{j}\}_{j=0}^{L-1} as a Markov chain (MC) with switching probabilities pj01≜Pr⁡{dj+1=0|dj=1}p_{j}^{01}\!\triangleq\!\Pr\{d_{j+1}\!=\!0\,|\,d_{j}\!=\!1\} and pj10≜Pr⁡{dj+1=1|dj=0}p_{j}^{10}\!\triangleq\!\Pr\{d_{j+1}\!=\!1\,|\,d_{j}\!=\!0\}. Here, pj01<0.5p_{j}^{01}<0.5 implies that the neighbors of a big xjx_{j} tend to be big, and pj10<0.5p_{j}^{10}<0.5 implies that the neighbors of a small xjx_{j} tend to be small. We note that {pj01,pj10}j=0L−1\{p_{j}^{01},p_{j}^{10}\}_{j=0}^{L-1} must be consistent with {λj}j=0L−1\{\lambda_{j}\}_{j=0}^{L-1} in that the following must hold for all jj:

[λj+1−λj+1]\displaystyle\begin{bmatrix}\lambda_{j+1}~&~1\!-\!\lambda_{j+1}\end{bmatrix} =\displaystyle= [λj−λj]​[−pj01pj01pj10−pj10].\displaystyle\begin{bmatrix}\lambda_{j}~&~1\!-\!\lambda_{j}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1\!-\!p_{j}^{01}&p_{j}^{01}\\ p_{j}^{10}&1\!-\!p_{j}^{10}\end{bmatrix}. (7)

Although we allow correlation among the tap states, we assume that the tap amplitudes are conditionally independent, i.e., p(xj+1,xj|dj+1,dj)=p(xj|dj)p(xj+1|dj+1)p(x_{j+1},x_{j}\,|\,d_{j+1},d_{j})\!=\!p(x_{j}\,|\,d_{j})p(x_{j+1}\,|\,d_{j+1}). Our experiences with IEEE 802.15.4a channels (see below) suggest that this is a valid assumption.

We emphasize that the model parameters {λj,pj01,pj01,νj1,νj0}\{\lambda_{j},p_{j}^{01},p_{j}^{01},\nu_{j}^{1},\nu_{j}^{0}\} are allowed to vary with lag jj, facilitating the exploitation of apriori known lag-dependencies in sparsity and/or clustering.

II-C An illustrative example: IEEE 802.15.4a channels

As an illustrative example of the clustered-sparse tap behavior described above, we generated realizations of the tap vector 𝒙≜[x0,…,xL−1]T\boldsymbol{x}\triangleq[x_{0},\dots,x_{L-1}]^{\textsf{T}} from channel impulse responses h⁡(τ)h(\tau) generated according to the method specified in the IEEE 802.15.4a “ultra-wideband” standard [16], which uses the Saleh-Valenzuela model [36]

h⁡(τ)\displaystyle h(\tau) =\displaystyle= ∑c=0C∑k=0Khk,c​ej​ϕk,c​δ​(τ−Tc−τk,c),\displaystyle\sum_{c=0}^{C}\sum_{k=0}^{K}h_{k,c}e^{j\phi_{k,c}}\delta(\tau-T_{c}-\tau_{k,c}), (8)

where CC denotes the number of clusters, TcT_{c} the delay of the ct​hc^{th} cluster, KK the number of components per cluster, {τk,c}\{\tau_{k,c}\} the relative component delays, {hk,c}\{h_{k,c}\} the component amplitudes, and {ϕk,c}\{\phi_{k,c}\} the component phases. In particular, the 802.15.4a standard specifies the following.

  • •

    The cluster arrival times are a Poisson process with rate Λ\Lambda, i.e., p⁡(Tc|Tc−1)=Λ​exp⁡(−Λ⁡(Tc−Tc−1))p(T_{c}\,|\,T_{c-1})\!=\!\Lambda\exp(-\Lambda(T_{c}-T_{c-1})). The initial cluster delay T0≥τminT_{0}\!\geq\!\tau_{\min}, as seen by the receiver, is a function of the timing synchronization algorithm.

  • •

    The component arrivals are a mixture of two Poisson processes: p⁡(τk,c|τk−1,c)=β​λ1​exp⁡(−λ1​(τk,c−τk−1,c))+(1−β)​λ2​exp⁡(−λ2​(τk,c−τk−1,c))p(\tau_{k,c}|\tau_{k-1,c})\!=\!\beta\lambda_{1}\exp(-\lambda_{1}(\tau_{k,c}-\tau_{k-1,c}))\!+\!(1-\beta)\lambda_{2}\exp(-\lambda_{2}(\tau_{k,c}-\tau_{k-1,c})) with τ0,c=0\tau_{0,c}=0.

  • •

    The component energies obey

    E⁡{|hk,c|2}\displaystyle\E\{|h_{k,c}|^{2}\} =\displaystyle= exp(−Tl/Γ−τk,l/γ)γ⁡[(1−β)​λ1+β​λ2+1],\displaystyle\frac{\exp(-T_{l}/\Gamma-\tau_{k,l}/\gamma)}{\gamma[(1-\beta)\lambda_{1}+\beta\lambda_{2}+1]}, (9)

    where Γ\Gamma is the cluster decay time constant and γ\gamma is the intra-cluster decay time constant.

  • •

    The amplitudes {hk,c}\{h_{k,c}\} are i.i.d Nakagami with mm-factors randomly generated via i.i.d m∼𝒩⁡(m0,m^02)m\sim\mathcal{N}(m_{0},\hat{m}^{2}_{0}).

  • •

    The phases {ϕk,c}\{\phi_{k,c}\} are i.i.d uniform on [0,2​π)[0,2\pi).

  • •

    The number of clusters, CC, is Poisson distributed with mean C¯\bar{C}, i.e., p⁡(C)=(C¯)C​exp⁡(−C¯)/(C!)p(C)\!=\!(\bar{C})^{C}\exp(-\bar{C})/(C!).

  • •

    The number of components per cluster, KK, is set large enough to yield a desired modeling accuracy.

Beyond the above specifications, we assume the following.

  • •

    The system bandwidth equals T−1=256T^{-1}=256 MHz.

    The number of taps (and CP length) was set at L=256L=256 (implying a maximal delay spread of 1​ν1\,\nusec) in order to capture all significant energy in h⁡(τ)h(\tau).

We now show results from an experiment conducted using U=10000U=10000 realizations of the tap vector 𝒙\boldsymbol{x}. In Fig. 1, we show histograms of Re⁡(xj)\real(x_{j}) for lags j∈{5,23,128,230}j\!\in\!\{5,23,128,230\}. and found that the magnitudes were <0.1<\!0.1, validating our assumption of conditionally independent tap amplitudes.

In summary, we see that IEEE 802.15.4a channels do indeed yield taps with the lag-dependent clustered sparsity described in Section II-B. Moreover, we have shown how the GM2-HMM parameters can be estimated from realizations of 𝒙\boldsymbol{x}. Next, we propose an efficient factor-graph based approach to joint channel-estimation and decoding (JCED) for BICM-OFDM using the GM2-HMM prior proposed in Section II-B.

III Joint Channel Estimation and Decoding

Our goal is to infer the information bits 𝒃\boldsymbol{b} from the OFDM observations 𝒚\boldsymbol{y} and the pilot/training bits 𝒄pt\boldsymbol{c}_{\textsf{pt}}, without knowing the channel state 𝒙\boldsymbol{x}. In particular, we aim to maximize the posterior pmf p⁡(bm|𝒚,𝒄pt)p(b_{m}\,|\,\boldsymbol{y},\boldsymbol{c}_{\textsf{pt}}) of each info bit. To exploit prior knowledge that 𝒙\boldsymbol{x} is clustered-sparse, we employ the GM2-HMM prior described in Section II-B. As a result, the info-bit posterior can be decomposed into the following product of factors:

p⁡(bm|𝒚,𝒄pt)=∑𝒃−mp⁡(𝒃|𝒚,𝒄pt)∝∑𝒃−mp⁡(𝒚|𝒃,𝒄pt)​p​(𝒃)\displaystyle p(b_{m}\,|\,\boldsymbol{y},\boldsymbol{c}_{\textsf{pt}})\,=\,\sum_{\boldsymbol{b}_{-m}}p(\boldsymbol{b}\,|\,\boldsymbol{y},\boldsymbol{c}_{\textsf{pt}})\,\propto\,\sum_{\boldsymbol{b}_{-m}}p(\boldsymbol{y}\,|\,\boldsymbol{b},\boldsymbol{c}_{\textsf{pt}})p(\boldsymbol{b}) (16)
=\displaystyle= ∫𝒙∑𝒔,𝒅,𝒄,𝒃−mp⁡(𝒚|𝒔,𝒙)​p​(𝒙|𝒅)​p​(𝒅)​p​(𝒔|𝒄)​p​(𝒄|𝒃,𝒄pt)​p​(𝒃)\displaystyle\int_{\boldsymbol{x}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{s},\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{c},\boldsymbol{b}_{-m}}\hskip-11.38109ptp(\boldsymbol{y}\,|\,\boldsymbol{s},\boldsymbol{x})p(\boldsymbol{x}\,|\,\boldsymbol{d})p(\boldsymbol{d})p(\boldsymbol{s}\,|\,\boldsymbol{c})p(\boldsymbol{c}\,|\,\boldsymbol{b},\boldsymbol{c}_{\textsf{pt}})p(\boldsymbol{b})
=\displaystyle= ∫𝒙∑𝒅∏j=0L−1p⁡(xj|dj)​p​(dj|dj−1)​∑𝒔∏i=0N−1p⁡(yi|si,𝒙)\displaystyle\int_{\boldsymbol{x}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{d}}\prod_{j=0}^{L-1}p(x_{j}\,|\,d_{j})p(d_{j}\,|\,d_{j-1})\sum_{\boldsymbol{s}}\prod_{i=0}^{N-1}p(y_{i}\,|\,s_{i},\boldsymbol{x})
×∑𝒄p⁡(si|𝒄i)​∑𝒃−mp⁡(𝒄|𝒃,𝒄pt)​∏m=1Mip⁡(bm),\displaystyle\mbox{}\times\sum_{\boldsymbol{c}}p(s_{i}\,|\,\boldsymbol{c}_{i})\sum_{\boldsymbol{b}_{-m}}p(\boldsymbol{c}\,|\,\boldsymbol{b},\boldsymbol{c}_{\textsf{pt}})\prod_{m=1}^{M_{\textsf{i}}}p(b_{m}),\quad (17)

where 𝒃−m≜[b1,…,bm−1,bm+1,…,bMi]T\boldsymbol{b}_{-m}\!\triangleq\![b_{1},\dots,b_{m-1},b_{m+1},\dots,b_{M_{\textsf{i}}}]^{\textsf{T}}. This factorization is illustrated by the factor graph in Fig. 4, where the round nodes represent random variables and the square nodes represent the factors of the posterior exposed in (17).

III-A Background on belief propagation

Although exact evaluation of the posteriors {p⁡(bm|𝒚,𝒄pt)}\{p(b_{m}\,|\,\boldsymbol{y},\boldsymbol{c}_{\textsf{pt}})\} is computationally impractical for the problem sizes of interest, these posteriors can be approximately evaluated using belief propagation (BP) [37] on the factor graph in Fig. 4. In textbook BP, beliefs take the form of pdfs/pmfs that are propagated among nodes of the factor graph via the sum/product algorithm (SPA) [18, 19, 20]:

  1. 1.

    Say the factor node ff is connected to the variable nodes {va}a=1A\{v_{a}\}_{a=1}^{A}. The belief passed from ff to vbv_{b} is pf→vb​(vb)∝∫{va}a≠bf⁡(v1,…,vA)​∏a≠bpva→f​(va)p_{f\rightarrow v_{b}}(v_{b})\propto\int_{\{v_{a}\}_{a\neq b}}f(v_{1},\dots,v_{A})\prod_{a\neq b}p_{v_{a}\rightarrow f}(v_{a}), given the beliefs {pva→f​(⋅)}a≠b\{p_{v_{a}\rightarrow f}(\cdot)\}_{a\neq b} recently passed to ff.

  2. 2.

    Say the variable node vv is connected to the factor nodes {f1,…,fB}\{f_{1},\dots,f_{B}\}. The belief passed from vv to faf_{a} is pv→fa​(v)∝∏b≠apfb→v​(v)p_{v\rightarrow f_{a}}(v)\propto\prod_{b\neq a}p_{f_{b}\rightarrow v}(v), given the beliefs {pfb→v​(⋅)}b≠a\{p_{f_{b}\rightarrow v}(\cdot)\}_{b\neq a} recently passed to vv.

  3. 3.

    Say the variable node vv is connected to the factor nodes {f1,…,fB}\{f_{1},\dots,f_{B}\}. The posterior on vv is the product of all recently arriving beliefs, i.e., p⁡(v)∝∏b=1Bpfb→v​(v)p(v)\propto\prod_{b=1}^{B}p_{f_{b}\rightarrow v}(v).

When the factor graph contains no loops, SPA-BP yields exact posteriors after two rounds of message passing (i.e., forward and backward). But, in the presence of loops, convergence to the exact posteriors is not guaranteed [25]. That said, there exist many problems to which loopy BP [37] has been successfully applied, including inference on Markov random fields [38], LDPC decoding [14], and compressed sensing [39, 40, 41, 13, 15, 32]. Our work not only leverages these past successes, but unites them.

III-B Background on GAMP

An important sub-problem within our larger bit-inference problem is the estimation of a vector of independent possibly-non-Gaussian variables 𝒙\boldsymbol{x} that are linearly mixed via 𝚽∈ℂN×L\boldsymbol{\Phi}\in{\mathbb{C}}^{N\times L} to form 𝒛=𝚽​𝒙=[z0,…,zN−1]T\boldsymbol{z}\!=\!\boldsymbol{\Phi x}\!=\![z_{0},\dots,z_{N-1}]^{\textsf{T}}, and subsequently observed as noisy measurements 𝒚\boldsymbol{y} through the possibly non-Gaussian pdfs {pYi|Zi(.|.)}i=0N−1\{p_{Y_{i}|Z_{i}}(.\,|\,.)\}_{i=0}^{N-1}. In our case, (6) specifies a GM2 prior on xjx_{j} and (4)—given the finite-alphabet uncertainty in sis_{i}—yields the non-Gaussian measurement pdf pYi|Zip_{Y_{i}|Z_{i}}. This “linear mixing” sub-problem is described by the factor graph shown within the middle dashed box in Fig. 4, where each node “yiy_{i}” represents the measurement pdf pYi|Zip_{Y_{i}|Z_{i}} and the node rightward of each node “xjx_{j}” represents the GM2 prior on xjx_{j}.

Building on recent work on multiuser detection by Guo and Wang [42], as well as recent work on message passing algorithms for compressed sensing by Donoho, Maleki, Montanari, and Bayati [40, 41], Rangan proposed a so-called generalized approximate message passing (GAMP) scheme that, for the sub-problem described above, admits rigorous analysis33 3 Since it is difficult to give a concise yet accurate account of GAMP’s technical properties, we refer the interested reader to [13]. as N,L→∞N,L\!\rightarrow\!\infty [13]. The main ideas behind GAMP are the following. First, although the beliefs flowing leftward from the nodes {xj}\{x_{j}\} are clearly non-Gaussian, the corresponding belief about zi=∑j=0L−1Φi​j​xjz_{i}=\sum_{j=0}^{L-1}\Phi_{ij}x_{j} can be accurately approximated as Gaussian, when LL is large, using the central limit theorem. Moreover, to calculate the parameters of this distribution (i.e., its mean and variance), only the mean and variance of each xjx_{j} are needed. Thus, it suffices to pass only means and variances leftward from each xjx_{j} node. It is similarly desirable to pass only means and variances rightward from each measurement node. Although the exact rightward flowing beliefs would be non-Gaussian (due to the non-Gaussian assumption on the measurement channels pYi|Zip_{Y_{i}|Z_{i}}), GAMP approximates them as Gaussian using a 2nd-order Taylor series, and passes only the resulting means and variances. A further simplification employed by GAMP is to approximate the differences among the outgoing means/variances of each left node, and the incoming means/variances of each right node, using Taylor series. The GAMP algorithm44 4 To be precise, the GAMP algorithm in Table I is an extension of that proposed in [13]. Table I handles circular complex-valued distributions and non-identically distributed signals and measurements. is summarized in Table I.

III-C Joint estimation and decoding using GAMP

We now detail our application of GAMP to joint channel-estimation and decoding (JCED) under the GM2-HMM tap prior, frequently referring to the factor graph in Fig. 4.

Because our factor graph is loopy, there exists considerable freedom in the message passing schedule. Roughly speaking, we choose to pass messages from the left to the right of Fig. 4 and back again, several times, stopping as soon as the messages converge. Each of these full cycles of message passing will be referred to as a “turbo iteration.” However, during a single turbo iteration, there may be multiple iterations of message passing between the GAMP and MC sub-graphs, which will be referred to as “equalizer” iterations. Furthermore, during a single equalizer iteration, there may be multiple iterations of message passing within the GAMP sub-graph, while there is at most one forward-backward iteration within the MC sub-graph. Finally, the SISO decoding block may itself be implemented using message passing, in which case it may also use several internal iterations. The message passing details are discussed below.

At the start of the first turbo iteration, there is total uncertainty about the information bits, so that Pr{bm=1}=12∀m\Pr\{b_{m}\!=\!1\}\!=\!\frac{1}{2}~\forall m. Thus, the initial bit beliefs flowing rightward out of the coding/interleaving block are uniformly distributed. Meanwhile, the pilot/training bits are known with certainty.

Coded-bit beliefs are then propagated rightward into the symbol mapping nodes. Since the symbol mapping is deterministic, the corresponding pdf factors take the form p⁡(s(k)|𝒄(l))=δk−lp(s^{(k)}\,|\,\boldsymbol{c}^{(l)})=\delta_{k-l}. The SPA dictates that the message passed rightward from symbol mapping node “ℳi\mathcal{M}_{i}” takes the form

pℳi→si​(s(k))\displaystyle p_{\mathcal{M}_{i}\rightarrow s_{i}}(s^{(k)}) ∝\displaystyle\propto ∑𝒄∈{0,1}Mp⁡(s(k)|𝒄)​∏m=1Mpci,m→ℳi​(cm)\displaystyle\sum_{\boldsymbol{c}\in\{0,1\}^{M}}p(s^{(k)}|\boldsymbol{c})\prod_{m=1}^{M}p_{c_{i,m}\rightarrow\mathcal{M}_{i}}(c_{m})\quad (18)
=\displaystyle= ∏m=1Mpci,m→ℳi​(cm(k)),\displaystyle\prod_{m=1}^{M}p_{c_{i,m}\rightarrow\mathcal{M}_{i}}(c_{m}^{(k)}), (19)

which is then copied forward as the message passed rightward from node sis_{i} (i.e., pℳi→si​(s(k))=psi→yi​(s(k))p_{\mathcal{M}_{i}\rightarrow s_{i}}(s^{(k)})=p_{s_{i}\rightarrow y_{i}}(s^{(k)})).

Recall, from Section III-B, that the symbol-belief passed rightward into the measurement node “yiy_{i}” determines the pdf pYi|Zip_{Y_{i}|Z_{i}} used in GAMP. Writing this symbol belief as 𝜷i≜[βi(1),…,βi(|𝕊|)]T\boldsymbol{\beta}_{i}\triangleq[\beta_{i}^{(1)},\dots,\beta_{i}^{(|\mathbb{S}|)}]^{\textsf{T}} for βi(k)≜psi→yi​(s(k))\beta_{i}^{(k)}\triangleq p_{s_{i}\rightarrow y_{i}}(s^{(k)}), equation (4) implies the measurement pdf

Above, ℒjapri\mathcal{L}_{j}^{\text{\sf apri}} is the apriori likelihood ratio Pr{dj=1}Pr{dj=0}\frac{\Pr\{d_{j}=1\}}{\Pr\{d_{j}=0\}} on the hidden state, ℒjext​(r^,νr)\mathcal{L}_{j}^{\text{\sf ext}}(\hat{r},\nu^{r}) is GAMP’s extrinsic likelihood ratio, and αj​(r^,νr)\alpha_{j}(\hat{r},\nu^{r}) is the corresponding posterior probability that dj=1d_{j}=1.

Using (21)-(30), the GAMP algorithm in Table I is iterated until it converges.55 5 More precisely, GAMP is iterated until the mean-square tap-estimate difference 1L​∑j=0L−1|x^j​(n)−x^j​(n−1)|2\frac{1}{L}\sum_{j=0}^{L-1}|\hat{x}_{j}(n)-\hat{x}_{j}(n-1)|^{2} falls below a threshold or a maximum number of GAMP iterations has elapsed. In doing so, GAMP generates (a close approximation to) both the conditional means 𝒙^\hat{\boldsymbol{x}} and variances 𝝂x≜[ν0x,…,νL−1x]T\boldsymbol{\nu}^{x}\!\triangleq\![\nu_{0}^{x},\dots,\nu_{L-1}^{x}]^{\textsf{T}} given the observations 𝒚\boldsymbol{y}, the soft symbol priors 𝜷≜[𝜷0,…,𝜷L−1]T\boldsymbol{\beta}\!\triangleq\![\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0},\dots,\boldsymbol{\beta}_{L-1}]^{\textsf{T}} and the sparsity prior 𝝀\boldsymbol{\lambda}. Conveniently, GAMP also returns (close approximations to) both the conditional means 𝒛^\hat{\boldsymbol{z}} and variances 𝝂z\boldsymbol{\nu}^{z} of the subchannel gains 𝒛\boldsymbol{z}, as well as posteriors 𝝃≜[𝝃0,…,𝝃L−1]T\boldsymbol{\xi}\!\triangleq\![\boldsymbol{\xi}_{0},\dots,\boldsymbol{\xi}_{L-1}]^{\textsf{T}} on the symbols 𝒔\boldsymbol{s}.

Before continuing, we discuss some GAMP details that are specific to our OFDM-JCED application. First, we notice that, to guarantee that the variance νiu​(n)\nu_{i}^{u}(n) in (R5) is positive, we must have νie<νz\nu^{e}_{i}\!<\!\nu_{z} in (22). Since this is not necessarily the case during the first few GAMP iterations, we clip νie\nu^{e}_{i} at the value 0.99​νz0.99\nu^{z}, where 0.990.99 was chosen heuristically. Second, due to unit-modulus property of the DFT elements Φi​j\Phi_{ij}, step (R2) in Table I simplifies to νiz​(n)=∑jνjx​(n)\nu^{z}_{i}(n)\!=\!\sum_{j}\nu_{j}^{x}(n) and (R6) simplifies to νjr​(n)=(∑iνiu​(n))−1\nu_{j}^{r}(n)\!=\!\big(\sum_{i}\nu_{i}^{u}(n)\big)^{-1}. With these simplifications, the complexity of GAMP is dominated by either the matrix-vector products ∑jΦi​j​x^j​(n)\sum_{j}\Phi_{ij}\hat{x}_{j}(n) in (R1) and ∑iΦi​j∗​u^i​(n)\sum_{i}\Phi_{ij}^{*}\hat{u}_{i}(n) in (R7), which can be implemented using a N​log2​NN\log_{2}N-multiply FFT when NN is a power-of-two, or by the calculation of {e^i,νie}i=0N−1\{\hat{e}_{i},\nu_{i}^{e}\}_{i=0}^{N-1} in (26)-(27), which requires 𝒪⁡(N​|𝕊|)\mathcal{O}(N|\mathbb{S}|) multiplies. Thus, GAMP requires only 𝒪⁡(N​log2​N+N​|𝕊|)\mathcal{O}(N\log_{2}N+N|\mathbb{S}|) multiplies per iteration.

After the messages within the GAMP sub-graph have converged, tap-state beliefs are passed rightward to the MC sub-graph. In particular, the SPA dictates that GAMP passes tap-state likelihoods or, equivalently, the extrinsic likelihood ratios ℒjext\mathcal{L}_{j}^{\text{\sf ext}}. Since the MC sub-graph is non-loopy, only one iteration of forward-backward message passing is performed,66 6 Message passing on the MC factor graph is a standard procedure. For details, we refer the reader to [14, 34]. after which the resulting tap-state likelihoods are passed leftward back to GAMP, where they are treated as tap-state priors 𝝀\boldsymbol{\lambda} in the next equalizer iteration. This interaction between the GAMP and MC sub-blocks can be recognized as an incarnation of the structured-sparse reconstruction scheme recently proposed by the authors in [15].

When the tap-state likelihoods passed between GAMP and MC have converged,77 7 More precisely, the equalizer iterations are terminated when the mean-square difference in tap-state log-likelihoods falls below a threshold or a maximum number of equalizer iterations has elapsed. the equalizer iterations are terminated and messages are passed leftward from the GAMP block. For this, SPA dictates that a symbol-belief propagates leftward from the yiy_{i} node with the form

psi←yi​(s)\displaystyle p_{s_{i}\leftarrow y_{i}}(s) ∝\displaystyle\propto ∫z𝒞​𝒩​(yi,s​z,νw)​𝒞​𝒩​(z,z^i,νiz)\displaystyle\int_{z}\mathcal{CN}(y_{i};sz,\nu^{w})\,\mathcal{CN}(z;\hat{z}_{i},\nu_{i}^{z}) (31)
=\displaystyle= 𝒞​𝒩​(yi,s​z^i,|s|2​νiz+νw),\displaystyle\mathcal{CN}(y_{i};s\hat{z}_{i},|s|^{2}\nu_{i}^{z}+\nu^{w}), (32)

where (z^i,νiz)(\hat{z}_{i},\nu_{i}^{z}) play the role of soft channel estimates. The SPA then implies that pℳi←si​(s)=psi←yi​(s)p_{\mathcal{M}_{i}\leftarrow s_{i}}(s)=p_{s_{i}\leftarrow y_{i}}(s).

Next, beliefs are passed leftward from each symbol-mapping node ℳi\mathcal{M}_{i} to the corresponding bit nodes ci,mc_{i,m}. From the SPA, they take the form

pci,m←ℳi​(c)\displaystyle p_{c_{i,m}\leftarrow\mathcal{M}_{i}}(c) (33)
∝\displaystyle\propto ∑k=1|𝕊|∑𝒄:cm=cp(s(k)|𝒄)pℳi←si(s(k))∏m′≠mpci,m′→ℳi(cm′)\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{|\mathbb{S}|}\sum_{\boldsymbol{c}:c_{m}=c}p(s^{(k)}\,|\,\boldsymbol{c})~p_{\mathcal{M}_{i}\leftarrow s_{i}}(s^{(k)})\prod_{m^{\prime}\neq m}p_{c_{i,m^{\prime}}\rightarrow\mathcal{M}_{i}}(c_{m^{\prime}})
=\displaystyle= ∑k:cm(k)=cpℳi←si(s(k))∏m′=1Mpci,m′→ℳi​(cm′(k))pci,m→ℳi​(c)\displaystyle\sum_{k:c_{m}^{(k)}=c}p_{\mathcal{M}_{i}\leftarrow s_{i}}(s^{(k)})\frac{\prod_{m^{\prime}=1}^{M}p_{c_{i,m^{\prime}}\rightarrow\mathcal{M}_{i}}(c_{m^{\prime}}^{(k)})}{p_{c_{i,m}\rightarrow\mathcal{M}_{i}}(c)}
=\displaystyle= 1pci,m→ℳi​(c)∑k:cm(k)=cpℳi←si(s(k))pℳi→si(s(k))\displaystyle\frac{1}{p_{c_{i,m}\rightarrow\mathcal{M}_{i}}(c)}\sum_{k:c_{m}^{(k)}=c}p_{\mathcal{M}_{i}\leftarrow s_{i}}(s^{(k)})p_{\mathcal{M}_{i}\rightarrow s_{i}}(s^{(k)}) (34)

for pairs (i,m)(i,m) that do not correspond to pilot/training bits. (Since the pilot/training bits are known with certainty, there is no need to update their pmfs.)

Finally, messages are passed leftward into the coding/interleaving block. Doing so is equivalent to feeding extrinsic soft bit estimates to a soft-input/soft-output (SISO) decoder/deinterleaver, which treats them as priors. Since SISO decoding is a well-studied topic [14, 43] and high-performance implementations are readily available (e.g., [44]), we will not elaborate on the details here. It suffices to say that, once the extrinsic outputs of the SISO decoder have been computed, they are re-interleaved and passed rightward from the coding/interleaving block to begin another turbo iteration. These turbo iterations continue until either the decoder detects no bit errors, the soft bit estimates have converged, or a maximum number of iterations has elapsed.

IV Numerical Results

In this section, we present numerical results that compare JCED using our GAMP-based scheme to that using soft-input soft-output (SISO) equalizers based on linear MMSE (LMMSE) and LASSO [9], as well as to performance bounds based on perfect channel state information (CSI).

IV-A Setup

For all results, we used irregular LDPC codes with codeword length ∼10000\sim\!10000 and average column weight 33, generated (and decoded) using the publicly available software [44], with random interleaving. We focus on the case of N=1024N\!=\!1024 subcarrier OFDM with 1616-QAM (i.e., M=4M\!=\!4) operating at a spectral efficiency of η=2\eta\!=\!2 bpcu. For bit-to-symbol mapping, we used multilevel Gray-mapping [45], noting recent work [46] that conjectures the optimality of Gray-mapping when BICM is used with a strong code. In some simulations, we used Np>0N_{\textsf{p}}\!>\!0 pilot-only subcarriers and Mt=0M_{\textsf{t}}\!=\!0 interspersed training bits, whereas in others we used Np=0N_{\textsf{p}}\!=\!0 and Mt>0M_{\textsf{t}}\!>\!0. When Np>0N_{\textsf{p}}\!>\!0, the pilot subcarriers were placed randomly and modulated with (known) QAM symbols chosen uniformly at random. When Mt>0M_{\textsf{t}}\!>\!0, the training bits were placed at the most significant bits (MSBs) of uniformly spaced data-subcarriers and modulated with the bit value 11.

Realizations of the tap vector 𝒙⁡[q]\boldsymbol{x}[q] were generated from IEEE 802.15.4a outdoor-NLOS impulse responses and SRRC pulses, as described in Section II-C, and not from the GM2-HMM model. The tap vectors generated for our simulations are thus as realistic as one can hope to obtain in software. All reported results are averaged over 50005000 channel realizations (i.e., 10710^{7} info bits).

The GM2-HMM parameters 𝝂0,𝝂1,𝒑01,𝒑10\boldsymbol{\nu}^{0},\boldsymbol{\nu}^{1},\boldsymbol{p}^{01},\boldsymbol{p}^{10} were fit from 1000010000 realizations of the tap-vector 𝒙\boldsymbol{x} using the procedure described in Section II-C. In doing so, we implicitly assumed88 8 If, instead, we knew that the receiver would be used in a different operating scenario, then we could generate representative realizations of 𝒙\boldsymbol{x} for that scenario and fit the GM2-HMM parameters accordingly. Furthermore, one could optimize the receiver for any desired balance between “typical” and “worst-case” operating conditions by simply choosing appropriate training realizations 𝒙\boldsymbol{x}. that the receiver is designed for the outdoor scenario, and we leverage the prior information made available by the extensive measurement campaign conducted for the IEEE 802.15.4a standard [16]. In all cases, we used a maximum of 1010 turbo iterations, 55 equalizer iterations, 1515 GAMP iterations, and 2525 LDPC decoder iterations, although in most cases the iterations converged early (as described in Section III-C).

IV-B Comparison with other schemes

The proposed GAMP-based equalizer was compared with soft-input soft-output (SISO) equalizers based on LMMSE and LASSO [9], whose constructions are now detailed.

All SISO equalizers are provided with the soft inputs 𝒔^​[q]\hat{\boldsymbol{s}}[q] and 𝝂s​[q]\boldsymbol{\nu}^{s}[q], i.e., the means and variances, respectively, of the symbols 𝒔⁡[q]∈𝕊N\boldsymbol{s}[q]\in\mathbb{S}^{N}. (Note that, if certain elements in 𝒔⁡[q]\boldsymbol{s}[q] are known perfectly as pilots, then the corresponding elements in 𝝂s​[q]\boldsymbol{\nu}^{s}[q] will be zero-valued.) Then, writing 𝒔​[q]=𝒔^​[q]+𝒔~​[q]\boldsymbol{s}[q]=\hat{\boldsymbol{s}}[q]+\tilde{\boldsymbol{s}}[q], where 𝒔~​[q]\tilde{\boldsymbol{s}}[q] an unknown zero-mean deviation, the subcarrier observations 𝒚⁡[q]=𝒟⁡(𝐬⁡[q])​𝚽​𝐱​[q]+𝐰⁡[q]\boldsymbol{y}[q]=\Diag(\boldsymbol{s}[q])\boldsymbol{\Phi}\boldsymbol{x}[q]+\boldsymbol{w}[q] can be written as

𝒚⁡[q]\displaystyle\boldsymbol{y}[q] =\displaystyle= 𝒟⁡(𝐬⁡[q])​𝚽​𝐱​[q]+𝐯⁡[q],\displaystyle\Diag(\boldsymbol{s}[q])\boldsymbol{\Phi}\boldsymbol{x}[q]+\boldsymbol{v}[q], (35)

where 𝒗⁡[q]≜𝒟⁡(𝐬~​[q])​𝚽​𝐱​[q]+𝐰⁡[q]\boldsymbol{v}[q]\triangleq\Diag(\tilde{\boldsymbol{s}}[q])\boldsymbol{\Phi}\boldsymbol{x}[q]+\boldsymbol{w}[q] is a zero-mean noise. Treating the elements within 𝒔~​[q]\tilde{\boldsymbol{s}}[q] as uncorrelated and doing the same with 𝒙⁡[q]\boldsymbol{x}[q], and leveraging the fact that 𝚽\boldsymbol{\Phi} is a truncated DFT matrix, it is straightforward to show that Cov⁡(𝒗⁡[q])=𝒟⁡(𝝂v​[q])\cov(\boldsymbol{v}[q])=\Diag(\boldsymbol{\nu}^{v}[q]) with 𝝂v​[q]=νw​𝟏+(𝟏T​𝝆)​𝝂s​[q]\boldsymbol{\nu}^{v}[q]=\nu^{w}\boldsymbol{1}+(\boldsymbol{1}^{\textsf{T}}\boldsymbol{\rho})\boldsymbol{\nu}^{s}[q], where 𝝆\boldsymbol{\rho} denotes the channel’s PDP. Without loss of generality, (35) can then be converted to the equivalent white-noise model

𝒖⁡[q]\displaystyle\boldsymbol{u}[q] ≜\displaystyle\triangleq 𝒟⁡(𝝂v​[q])−12​𝐲​[q]=𝐀𝐱⁡[q]+𝐧⁡[q],\displaystyle\Diag(\boldsymbol{\nu}^{v}[q])^{-\frac{1}{2}}\boldsymbol{y}[q]=\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}[q]+\boldsymbol{n}[q], (36)

where Cov⁡(𝒏⁡[q])=𝑰\cov(\boldsymbol{n}[q])=\boldsymbol{I} and 𝑨⁡[q]≜𝒟⁡(𝝂v​[q]−12​𝐬​[q])​𝚽\boldsymbol{A}[q]\triangleq\Diag(\boldsymbol{\nu}^{v}[q]^{-\frac{1}{2}}\boldsymbol{s}[q])\boldsymbol{\Phi} is a known matrix. In summary, (36) provides a mechanism to handle soft inputs for both LASSO and LMMSE.

For LMMSE equalization, we first used (36) to compute

𝒙^lmmse​[q]\displaystyle\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}_{\text{\sf lmmse}}[q] =\displaystyle= 𝒟⁡(𝝆)​𝐀H​[q]​(𝐀⁡[q]​𝒟⁡(𝝆)​𝐀H​[q]+𝐈)−1​𝐮​[q]\displaystyle\Diag(\boldsymbol{\rho})\boldsymbol{A}^{\textsf{H}}[q]\big(\boldsymbol{A}[q]\Diag(\boldsymbol{\rho})\boldsymbol{A}^{\textsf{H}}[q]+\boldsymbol{I}\big)^{-1}\boldsymbol{u}[q]\quad (37)

from which we obtain the subcarrier gain estimate 𝒛^lmmse​[q]=𝚽​𝒙^lmmse​[q]\hat{\boldsymbol{z}}_{\text{\sf lmmse}}[q]=\boldsymbol{\Phi}\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}_{\text{\sf lmmse}}[q]. The covariance matrix of 𝒛^lmmse​[q]\hat{\boldsymbol{z}}_{\text{\sf lmmse}}[q] is [2]

𝚽⁡(𝒟⁡(𝝆)−𝒟⁡(𝝆)​𝐀H​[q]​(𝐀⁡[q]​𝒟⁡(𝝆)​𝐀H​[q]+𝐈)−1​𝐀​[q]​𝒟⁡(𝝆))​𝚽H\boldsymbol{\Phi}\big(\!\Diag(\boldsymbol{\rho})-\Diag(\boldsymbol{\rho})\boldsymbol{A}^{\textsf{H}}[q]\big(\boldsymbol{A}[q]\Diag(\boldsymbol{\rho})\boldsymbol{A}^{\textsf{H}}[q]+\boldsymbol{I}\big)^{-1}\boldsymbol{A}[q]\Diag(\boldsymbol{\rho})\!\big)\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{\textsf{H}}

whose diagonal elements 𝝂lmmsez​[q]\boldsymbol{\nu}^{z}_{\text{\sf lmmse}}[q] are variances on the gain estimates 𝒛^lmmse​[q]\hat{\boldsymbol{z}}_{\text{\sf lmmse}}[q]. Finally, we obtain soft symbol estimates from the soft gain estimates (𝒛^lmmse​[q],𝝂lmmsez​[q])(\hat{\boldsymbol{z}}_{\text{\sf lmmse}}[q],\boldsymbol{\nu}^{z}_{\text{\sf lmmse}}[q]) via (32).

For LASSO,99 9 The criterion employed by LASSO [9] is equivalent to the one employed in “basis pursuit denoising” [10]. we first computed the tap estimate 𝒙^lasso​[q]\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}_{\text{\sf lasso}}[q] from (36) using the celebrated SPGL1 algorithm [47]. In doing so, we needed to specify the target residual variance, i.e., νlassou≜1N​‖𝒖⁡[q]−𝑨⁡[q]​𝒙^lasso​[q]‖22\nu^{u}_{\text{\sf lasso}}\!\triangleq\!\frac{1}{N}\|\boldsymbol{u}[q]-\boldsymbol{A}[q]\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}_{\text{\sf lasso}}[q]\|_{2}^{2}. Because Cov⁡(𝒏⁡[q])=𝑰\cov(\boldsymbol{n}[q])=\boldsymbol{I}, we expect the optimal value of νlassou\nu^{u}_{\text{\sf lasso}} to be near 11 and, after extensive experimentation, we found that the value νlassou=0.9\nu^{u}_{\text{\sf lasso}}\!=\!0.9 works well at high SNR and that the value νlassou=1.5\nu^{u}_{\text{\sf lasso}}\!=\!1.5 works well at low SNR. Thus, for each 𝒖⁡[q]\boldsymbol{u}[q], we computed SPGL1 estimates using each of these two1010 10 We also tried running SPGL1 for a dense grid of νlassou\nu^{u}_{\text{\sf lasso}} values, but often it would get “stuck” at one of them and eventually return an error. targets, and kept the one that minimized the squared error νlassox​[q]≜1L​‖𝒙⁡[q]−𝒙^lasso​[q]‖22\nu^{x}_{\text{\sf lasso}}[q]\triangleq\frac{1}{L}\|\boldsymbol{x}[q]-\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}_{\text{\sf lasso}}[q]\|_{2}^{2}, which we assume a genie is able to provide. For the soft outputs, we set 𝒛^lasso​[q]=𝚽​𝒙^lasso​[q]\hat{\boldsymbol{z}}_{\text{\sf lasso}}[q]=\boldsymbol{\Phi}\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}_{\text{\sf lasso}}[q] and take 𝝂lassoz​[q]\boldsymbol{\nu}^{z}_{\text{\sf lasso}}[q] to be the diagonal elements of 𝚽​Cov⁡(𝒙^lasso​[q])​𝚽H\boldsymbol{\Phi}\cov(\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}_{\text{\sf lasso}}[q])\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{\textsf{H}}. Assuming Cov⁡(𝒙^lasso​[q])=νlassox​[q]​𝑰\cov(\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}_{\text{\sf lasso}}[q])=\nu^{x}_{\text{\sf lasso}}[q]\boldsymbol{I} and leveraging the fact that 𝚽\boldsymbol{\Phi} is a truncated DFT matrix, we find 𝝂lassoz​[q]=L​νlassox​[q]​𝟏\boldsymbol{\nu}^{z}_{\text{\sf lasso}}[q]=L\nu^{x}_{\text{\sf lasso}}[q]\boldsymbol{1}. Finally, using (32), we obtain soft symbol estimates from the soft gain estimates (𝒛^lasso​[q],𝝂lassoz​[q])(\hat{\boldsymbol{z}}_{\text{\sf lasso}}[q],\boldsymbol{\nu}^{z}_{\text{\sf lasso}}[q]). Due to the genie-aided steps, the performance attained by our LASSO implementation is better than what could be obtained in practice.

These LMMSE- and LASSO-based SISO equalizers were then embedded in the overall factor graph in the same manner as GAMP, with the following exceptions: 1) The LMMSE and LASSO algorithms could not be connected to the MC sub-block, since they are not based on a two-state mixture model; 2) For LASSO, if the genie-aided MSE νlassox​[q]\nu^{x}_{\text{\sf lasso}}[q] did not improve during a given turbo iteration, then the corresponding outputs (𝒛^lasso​[q],𝝂lassoz​[q])(\hat{\boldsymbol{z}}_{\text{\sf lasso}}[q],\boldsymbol{\nu}^{z}_{\text{\sf lasso}}[q]) were not updated. This rule was employed to prevent turbo-LASSO from occasionally diverging at low SNR; 3) For LASSO, if Np>0N_{\textsf{p}}\!>\!0 and Mt=0M_{\textsf{t}}\!=\!0, then the LASSO estimates computed during the first turbo iteration use only pilot subcarriers. This makes the performance of SISO-LASSO after the first turbo iteration equal to the performance of the standard pilot-aided LASSO.

IV-C BER versus the number of pilot subcarriers NpN_{\textsf{p}}

Figure 5 shows bit error rate (BER) versus the number of pilot subcarriers NpN_{\textsf{p}} at Eb/No=11E_{b}/N_{o}\!=\!11 dB and a fixed spectral efficiency of η=2\eta\!=\!2 bpcu. In this and other figures, “ALG-#” refers to algorithm ALG with # turbo iterations (and “ALG-fin” after turbo convergence; see Fig. 10) with the MC block disconnected (i.e., there was no attempt to exploit tap clustering). Meanwhile “GAMP-# MC-5” refers to GAMP+MC after # turbo iterations, each containing 55 equalizer iterations. Finally, PCSI refers to MAP equalization under perfect CSI, which yields a bound on the BER performance of any equalizer.

The curves in Fig. 5 exhibit a “U” shape because, as NpN_{\textsf{p}} increases, the code rate RR must decrease to maintain the fixed spectral efficiency η=2\eta=2 bpcu. While an increase in NpN_{\textsf{p}} generally makes channel estimation easier, the reduction in RR makes data decoding more difficult. For all schemes under comparison, Fig. 5 suggests that the choice Np≈224N_{\textsf{p}}\!\approx\!224 is optimal under the operating conditions. Overall, we see GAMP significantly outperforming both LMMSE and LASSO. Moreover, we see a small but definite gain from the MC block.

IV-D BER versus the number of interspersed training bits MtM_{\textsf{t}}

Although Np>0N_{\textsf{p}}>0 pilot subcarriers are required for decoupled channel estimation and decoding, JCED can function with Np=0N_{\textsf{p}}\!=\!0 as long as a sufficient number MtM_{\textsf{t}} of training bits are interspersed among the coded bits used to construct each QAM symbol. To examine this latter case, Fig. 6 shows BER versus MtM_{\textsf{t}} at Eb/No=10E_{b}/N_{o}\!=\!10 dB, a fixed spectral efficiency of η=2\eta\!=\!2 bpcu, and Np=0N_{\textsf{p}}\!=\!0. Again we see the “U” shape, but with GAMP working very well for a relatively wide range of MtM_{\textsf{t}}, and again we see a small but noticeable BER improvement when the MC block is used. SISO-LASSO seems to work to some degree with Np=0N_{\textsf{p}}=0, but SISO-LASSO does not.

IV-E BER versus Eb/NoE_{b}/N_{o}

Figure 7 shows BER versus Eb/NoE_{b}/N_{o} using Np=224N_{\textsf{p}}\!=\!224 pilot subcarriers (as suggested by Fig. 5) and Mt=0M_{\textsf{t}}\!=\!0 training bits. Relative to the perfect-CSI bound, we see SISO-LASSO performing within 55 dB during the first turbo iteration and within 4.54.5 dB after convergence. Meanwhile, we see SISO-LMMSE performing very poorly during the first turbo iteration, but eventually surpassing SISO-LASSO and coming within 44 dB from the perfect-CSI bound. Remarkably, we see GAMP+MC performing within 0.60.6 dB of the perfect-CSI bound (and within 11 dB after only 22 turbo iterations). This excellent performance confirms that the proposed GM2-HMM channel model and equalizer design together do an excellent job of capturing and exploiting the lag-dependent clustered-sparse characteristics of the 802.15.4a channel taps. Comparing the GAMP traces to the GAMP+MC traces, we see that the MC block yields a small but noticeable benefit.

Figure 8 shows BER versus Eb/NoE_{b}/N_{o} using Mt=448M_{\textsf{t}}\!=\!448 interspersed training bits (as suggested by Fig. 6) and Np=0N_{\textsf{p}}\!=\!0 pilot subcarriers. There we see that SISO-LASSO does not perform well at all. SISO-LMMSE works to some degree after several turbo iterations, although not as well as in the Np>0N_{\textsf{p}}>0 case. Meanwhile, we see GAMP+MC performing within 11 dB of the perfect-CSI case, and GAMP alone performing within 1.51.5 dB. Comparing Fig. 8 to Fig. 7, we see GAMP with training bits performing about 11 dB better than GAMP with dedicated pilot subcarriers. The perfect-CSI bound likewise improves because, with 1616-QAM, Mt=448M_{\textsf{t}}\!=\!448 training bits constitutes half the overhead of Np=224N_{\textsf{p}}\!=\!224 pilot subcarriers, allowing Fig. 8 the use of a stronger code at η=2\eta\!=\!2 bpcu.

IV-F Channel-tap NMSE versus Eb/NoE_{b}/N_{o}

Figure 9 shows the channel estimates’ normalized mean-squared error (NMSE) E⁡{‖𝒙⁡[q]−𝒙^​[q]‖22/‖𝒙⁡[q]‖22}\E\{\|\boldsymbol{x}[q]\!-\!\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}[q]\|_{2}^{2}/\|\boldsymbol{x}[q]\|_{2}^{2}\} versus Eb/NoE_{b}/N_{o}, at the point that the turbo iterations were terminated, using Np=224N_{\textsf{p}}\!=\!224 pilot subcarriers and Mt=0M_{\textsf{t}}\!=\!0 training bits. (For comparison, Fig. 7 shows BER for this configuration.) We also show the NMSE attained by the “bit and support genie” (BSG), which calculates MMSE channel estimates using perfect knowledge of both the coded bits and the hidden channel states {dj}\{d_{j}\}, and which provides a lower bound for any channel estimator. In the figure, we see that the NMSEs of LMMSE and LASSO channel estimates are within 88-to-1212 dB of the BSG, whereas those of GAMP are within 22-to-44 dB. Meanwhile, we see that GAMP+MC has a small but noticeable advantage over GAMP alone. We reason that the LMMSE estimates are worse than the GAMP estimates because they do not exploit the non-Gaussianity of the channel taps xjx_{j}, and the LASSO estimates are worse than the GAMP estimates because they do not exploit the known priors on the channel taps (i.e., the lag-dependent sparsity 𝝀\boldsymbol{\lambda} and PDP 𝝆\boldsymbol{\rho}).

IV-G Computational complexity versus Eb/NoE_{b}/N_{o}

Figure 10 shows the average time per turbo iteration (in Matlab seconds on a 2.62.6GHz CPU), the average number of turbo iterations, and the average total time (to turbo convergence), as a function of Eb/NoE_{b}/N_{o}, using Np=224N_{\textsf{p}}\!=\!224 pilot subcarriers and Mt=0M_{\textsf{t}}\!=\!0 training bits. (For comparison, Fig. 7 shows BER for this configuration and Fig. 9 shows NMSE.) Regarding the average time per turbo iteration, we see GAMP±\pmMC taking ≈1.5\approx 1.5 sec at low Eb/NoE_{b}/N_{o} and ≈0.5\approx 0.5 sec at high Eb/NoE_{b}/N_{o}. GAMP+MC takes only slightly longer than GAMP alone due to the efficiency of the message computations within the MC block, and the fact that both the GAMP iterations and equalizer iterations are terminated as soon as the messages converge. In comparison, SISO-LMMSE takes ≈4.5\approx 4.5 sec per turbo iteration, and SISO-LASSO takes between 11 and 77 sec, depending on Eb/NoE_{b}/N_{o}. Regarding the number of average number of turbo iterations until convergence, we see that—at low Eb/NoE_{b}/N_{o}—GAMP+MC takes about 55 turbo iterations, GAMP alone takes about 77, SISO-LMMSE takes about 55, and SISO-LASSO takes about 33, while—at high Eb/NoE_{b}/N_{o}—all algorithms converge after only 11 turbo iteration. Regarding the total time for equalization, GAMP+MC and GAMP are about the same at low Eb/NoE_{b}/N_{o}, whereas GAMP alone takes about 30%30\% less time at high Eb/NoE_{b}/N_{o}. Meanwhile, SISO-LASSO and SISO-LMMSE are uniformly slower than GAMP and GAMP+MC over the entire Eb/NoE_{b}/N_{o} range, in some cases by a factor of 1010.

V Conclusion

In this paper, we presented a factor-graph approach to joint channel-estimation and decoding (JCED) for BICM-OFDM that merges recent advances in approximate message passing algorithms [13] with those in structured-sparse signal reconstruction [15] and SISO decoding [14]. Different from existing factor-graph approaches to JCED, ours is able to exploit not only sparse channel taps, but also clustered sparsity patterns that typify large-bandwidth communication channels, such as those that result from pulse-shaped communication over IEEE 802.15.4a modeled channels. For this purpose, we proposed the use of a two-state Gaussian mixture prior with a Markov model on the hidden tap states. The implementation complexity of our JCED scheme is dominated by 𝒪⁡(N​log2​N+N​|𝕊|)\mathcal{O}(N\log_{2}N\!+\!N|\mathbb{S}|) multiplies per GAMP iteration, facilitating the application to systems with many subcarriers NN and many channel taps L<NL<N. Experiments with IEEE 802.15.4a modeled channels showed BER performance within 11 dB of the known-channel bound, and 33–44 dB better than LMMSE- and LASSO-based soft equalizers. These experiments also suggested that, with our proposed approach, the use of interspersed training bits is more efficient than the use of dedicated pilot subcarriers. For very large constellations (e.g., |𝕊|=1024|\mathbb{S}|\!=\!1024), future work is motivated to reduce the linear complexity dependence on |𝕊||\mathbb{S}|.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
